svg.aria-label: How to write 假: 11 strokes · 10 pen lifts · 11 movements
svg.title: Writing 假
svg.desc: 11 frames; frame N shows movements 1 to N of 假 (chinese), the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished letter, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansSC-Subset.ttf. Stroke order after Hanzi Writer Data 假.json, ordered stroke paths and medians 1–11 (Hanzi Writer Data snapshot 68d10a4, updated from Make Me a Hanzi, 22 June 2019) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chanind/hanzi-writer-data/68d10a4b21150cae5e1ebbd223eed289cf32d90c/data/%E5%81%87.json>. Source note on variation: The cited PRC-order dataset supplies eleven ordered strokes for 假, in three pieces. Medians 1–2 draw the person piece on the left as 你 opens: a left-falling stroke, then a vertical. Medians 3–7 draw the middle piece: a short horizontal that turns down without lifting, a short horizontal under it, a long vertical down the left side, then two short horizontals against it, the upper one first. Medians 8–11 draw the right piece: a short horizontal that turns down without lifting, a short horizontal under it, a horizontal that turns and sweeps down to the left without lifting, then a long right-falling stroke across it. Make Me a Hanzi documents that its stroke paths are ordered in proper stroke order, its medians use the same coordinate system for stroke-order animation, and the project follows People's Republic of China stroke order. This learner path adapts those eleven ordered medians to the vendored Noto Sans SC outline while preserving their order, their directions, the turns and ten intervening pen lifts; stroke widths and proportions differ between the Arphic-derived source graphics and Noto Sans SC.
